The graph of $y=f(x)$ is shown above. Which of the following could be the graph of $y={f}^{′}(x)$, the derivative of $f(x)?$
questions.worked_solution:
Notice the following:

- At the stationary points, where the tangent line to $y=f(x)$ is parallel to the $x$-axis, we have ${f}^{′}(x)=0.$

- When $f(x)$ is increasing, we have ${f}^{′}(x)>0.$

- When $f(x)$ is decreasing, we have ${f}^{′}(x)<0.$

We can now summarize the information from the graph in the table below. Note that the stationary point was identified (approximately) from the graph of $y=f(x)$:

| $x$ | $(-\infty ,2.5)$ | $2.5$ | $(2.5,\infty )$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $f$ | $↘$ | $\text{min}$ | $↗$ |
| ${f}^{′}$ | $-$ | $0$ | $+$ |

Additionally, from the graph of $y=f(x),$ we can conclude that there are no inflection points.  Also, the graph of $y=f(x)$ is concave up in $(-\infty ,\infty ).$ So, ${f}^{″}(x)>0$ and $y={f}^{′}(x)$ is increasing.

Therefore, the graph of $y={f}^{′}(x)$ may look as shown below.

The graph of $y=f(x)$ is shown above. Which of the following could be the graph of $y={f}^{′}(x)$, the derivative of $f(x)?$
questions.worked_solution:
Since the function is piecewise-linear, we get a constant derivative over each linear part.
Notice the following:

- When $f(x)$ is decreasing, we get ${f}^{′}(x)<0.$

- When $f(x)$ is constant, we get ${f}^{′}(x)=0.$

We can now summarize the information from the graph in the table below.

| $x$ | $(-\infty ,0)$ | $0$ | $(0,\infty )$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $f$ | $\text{const.}$ | $\text{max}$ | $↘$ |
| ${f}^{′}$ | $0$ | $\text{undef.}$ | $-$ |

From the graph of $y=f(x),$ we can conclude that there are no inflection points. 

Additionally, we have a change of the slope of the tangent line (from  $0$ to negative)  when we pass through $x=0$ from left to right. This means that the derivative is not defined at $x=0$ and we obtain a jump discontinuity at this point for the graph of $y={f}^{′}(x).$ 

Therefore, the graph of $y={f}^{′}(x)$ may look as shown below.

canonical_examples.problem:
The graph of the function $y=f'(x)$, the derivative of $y=f(x)$, is shown below. Sketch the graph of $y=f''(x).$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14190876/assets/bf8bde9f9b5060fbf14a329833f35ce9970c850e805e0c551cccaa70d6288c06.png)
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, if we denote $g(x) = f'(x)$ then $f''(x)=g'(x).$ So, we need to sketch the graph of $y=g'(x)$ given the graph of $y=g(x),$ as usual.

Notice the following:

- At the critical points, where the tangent line to $y=f(x)$ is parallel to the $x$-axis, we have $g'(x)=0.$

- When $f(x)$ is increasing, we have $g'(x)>0.$

- When $f(x)$ is decreasing, we have $g'(x) < 0.$

We can now summarize the information from the graph in the table below. Note that the critical points were identified (approximately) from the graph of $y=g(x)$:

| $x$ | $(-\infty,1)$ | $1$ | $(1,3)$ | $3$ | $(3,\infty)$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $g$ | $\searrow$ | $\textrm{not extr.}$ | $\searrow$ | $\textrm{min}$ | $\nearrow$ |
| $g'$ | $-$ | $0$ | $-$ | $0$ | $+$ |

Additionally, the function has an inflection point at $x \approx 1$ and $x\approx 2.25.$ At the inflection points, we have $g''(x)=0,$ so the tangent to the graph of $y=g'(x)$ must be parallel to the $x$-axis at $x\approx 1$ and $x\approx 2.25.$

We don't know the exact value of $g'(1)$ and $g'(2.25),$ but from the graph of $y=g(x),$ we can conclude that at $x \approx 1$ and $x\approx 2.25$ the slope is zero and negative, respectively.

Therefore, the graph of $y=g'(x)=f''(x)$ may look as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14190876/assets/785b221ae245b389e707f8189c91e57af888ecbb44dfce384ab1c60958d91a6f.png)

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
Suppose we are given the graph of the function $f(x),$ as shown below. The function has critical points at $x=-1,$ $x=2,$ and an inflection point at $x=0.5.$
How can we sketch the graph of the derivative $f'(x)?$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14190876/assets/b3fcc7a08d2a083567cc2de62c9bb0c6e9516552c8a2f08d2e814604f5ec84f8.png)

Notice the following:

- At the stationary points, where the tangent line to $y=f(x)$ is parallel to the $x$-axis, we have $f'(x)=0.$

- When $f(x)$ is increasing, we have $f'(x) > 0.$

- When $f(x)$ is decreasing, we have $f'(x) < 0.$

We can now summarize the information from the graph in the table below:

| $x$ | $(-\infty,-1)$ | $-1$ | $(-1,2)$ | $2$ | $(2,\infty)$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $f$ | $\nearrow$ | $\textrm{max}$ | $\searrow$ | $\textrm{min}$ | $\nearrow$ |
| $f'$ | $+$ | $0$ | $-$ | $0$ | $+$ |

Using this information, we can identify the regions where $f'(x)$ should cross the $x$-axis. According to the table, these are points $(-1,0)$ and $(2,0)\mathbin{:}$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14190876/assets/e98d21084e06d2a28509b0b68f449c5f42959ee1adad9b3dbf912885968a3b33.png)

Additionally, we are told that the function has an inflection point at $x = 0.5.$ So $f''(0.5)=0$ and the tangent to the graph of $y=f'(x)$ must be parallel to the $x$-axis.

We don't know the exact value of $f'(0.5)$ but from the graph of $y=f(x),$ we can conclude that at $x = 0.5$ the slope is negative. Therefore, we get a point below the $x$-axis:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14190876/assets/5994a9139fbd1c530692a2fb40b2fb1b4b7bd0b34b2bf7ff7194390542748977.png)

Finally, connecting up the parts of the graph above, we get an approximate sketch of $f'(x)\mathbin{:}$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14190876/assets/f21fca7744d7196e457f0a9d4511f644a3cf1e8c61018c152fc74ea7f6999f3e.png)
